candidate.document:
Otieno had been composing the email since Tuesday. His sister Akinyi, who worked in a lawyer's office in Upper Hill, read it over his shoulder on the matatu.

"'Dear Sir or Madam, I humbly wish to inform you of my intention to commence physical exercise,'" she read aloud. "You sound like you're surrendering."

"It's formal."

"It's a gym, Oti. Say what you want."

He deleted it and typed: *Hello. I want to start the 3 month membership. When can I come?* Then, after a pause, he added: *I have not run since Form Three.*

"Why would you tell them that?"

"So they know."

The reply came before they reached Kenyatta Avenue. It was from someone called Mercy Wambui, Front Desk.

*Hi Otieno. Welcome. You can start Monday. The manager says I should offer you the 12 month package because it works out cheaper per month. That is true. But I also see the sign-in sheets. Most people who buy 12 months come for six weeks and then I see them at Naivas buying chapati. Do the 3 months. If you're still coming in week ten, I'll tell you about the annual one myself and you'll actually use it. Bring water. Do not wear jeans, someone did.*

Akinyi read it twice. "She'll be fired."

"She told me the cheaper thing too. She didn't hide it."

"She called you lazy."

"She called everyone lazy. That's different."

He wrote back: *Thank you. 3 months. Monday.* Then, after another pause: *What time is it least embarrassing?*

*6 a.m.,* Mercy replied. *Only the pastors and the night guards. Nobody looks at anybody.*

Akinyi was already scrolling her own phone. "What's the gym called again?"
